# Coding guide

Apply these rules to every file you write or edit, tests included. Language guides refine these
rules for their language. Follow explicit user instructions and repository conventions over these
defaults.

## Write straightforward code

- Before writing code, ask whether it needs to exist. Skip work for a need nobody has shown.
- Prefer deleting code over adding it.
- Use descriptive names. No abbreviations, even idiomatic: `getUserByIdentifier` not `getUsr`, and
  no `btn`, `cb`, or `errMsg`.
- Search for an existing helper before writing one. Reuse or extend it when it serves the same
  purpose.
- Use the standard library or an installed dependency before adding one.
- Fix a bug once at its root cause, in the function all callers share, not only the caller the
  report names.
- Parse untrusted values once at the boundary and pass trusted types inward. Follow
  [ADR 0005](./adr/0005-results-and-parse-once.md) for results and parsing.
- Reject invalid states where they enter the system, and report the error there.
- Check each reason to reject in its own guard, with its own error message.

## Drop backwards compatibility by default

Follow [ADR 0008](./adr/0008-backwards-compatibility.md) for compatibility and saved formats.

- On an interface change, update its callers in the repository and delete the old path.
- Do not keep deprecated aliases, optional parameters for the old call shape, branches for old
  config keys, or re-exports of moved symbols.
- Ask before choosing when something outside the repository may use the old surface: a published
  package, API, or CLI, a user config file, or data an earlier version saved.
- If deleting the old path is outside the task, say so instead of silently keeping both.

## Keep functions small

Follow [ADR 0009](./adr/0009-advisory-review-signals.md) for size review signals.

- One function, one job. Split anything that does two.
- Review functions over 60 lines, files over 500 lines, and functions with more than 4 parameters.
- Keep related control flow and state together when splitting hurts traceability.
- Do not add inheritance or parameter objects only to meet a size threshold.
- Extract a phase or callback when its name and boundary make the caller clearer.
- Declare a helper before the function that uses it. Do not define one in the middle of unrelated
  steps.
- When a linter flags complexity, simplify first. Suppress narrowly with a comment explaining why.

## Separate logical steps

- Separate the logical steps in every function with one blank line, never two.

## Keep conditions short

- Join at most 3 checks in one condition and move the rest into named booleans or predicates, one
  per idea: `escapesRepository(file)` not `file === '..' || file.startsWith('../')`.
- Do not mix "and" with "or" in one condition. Name the inner group first.
- When a condition appears twice, replace both with one named predicate.

## Keep statements readable

- Give each statement one job. Split a line that computes a value and also decides what to do with
  it.
- Assign call chains and ternaries to named variables before using them in arguments, conditions,
  templates, or literals.
- Spread a ternary only for an optional property: `...(model === undefined ? {} : { model })`.
- Build lists with optional items step by step: `push` each in its own `if`, or spread a helper
  returning `[]` when absent.

## Comment only what the code cannot say

- Default to no comment or doc comment. Add one only when a reader would otherwise make a wrong
  change: a constraint, invariant, workaround, or surprising behavior the code cannot show.
- State the rule itself: never cite an ADR, ticket, PR, or review, and never describe the code's
  history.
- Never state a cause or measurement you have not checked in this session, even if a ticket says it.
- Never restate the name, type, or signature below the comment.
- Match the comment density and style already in the file.
- Keep required documentation and tool directives. Delete commented-out code and temporary notes.

## Write tests that can fail

Follow [ADR 0007](./adr/0007-test-placement-and-fakes.md) for test placement and fakes, and
[ADR 0006](./adr/0006-side-effect-records.md) for side-effect records.

- Make each test defend one observable behavior: an output, a state change, or an error. If you
  cannot say what breaks for the caller, do not write it.
- When code must refuse, assert the error and that nothing else changed.
- Do not assert inside a fake or callback whose errors the production code may catch. Record the
  value and assert after the call.
- Before refactoring, reuse useful coverage or add a characterization test or equivalence check of
  observable behavior that passes before and after. Do not force a failing test. For a rename, also
  check strings, docs, and serialized names.

## Decide when a module gets a property test

A property test generates inputs or call orders and checks one rule against each of them.

- Write a property test for a module when one of these triggers holds:
  - Its output depends on state from earlier calls, such as dedupe, retry, cancellation, ownership,
    or queues.
  - A bug in it was caused by event order.
  - One of its functions has a law: a round trip, idempotence, or agreement with a simpler oracle.
- When a trigger holds and you write no property test, state in one PR line why examples are enough.
- When no trigger holds, the PR needs no such line.

# TypeScript coding guide

Apply these rules with the [general coding guide](../../shared/coding.md) to every TypeScript file,
tests included.

## Types

Follow [ADR 0005](../../shared/adr/0005-results-and-parse-once.md) for results, errors, and parsing.

- Model variants as a discriminated union, not as a bag of optional fields or a second boolean that
  must stay in sync with the first.
- Use the simplest total type. Make a type stricter, such as `[T, ...T[]]`, only where the loose
  type forces a `!`, a cast, or a "should never happen" throw.
- Infer types from the repository's schema library, such as TypeBox `Static<typeof Schema>`, before
  you write a type guard by hand.
- A type guard must check every claim its type makes.
- Brand a primitive only when a concrete signature shows a real risk of mixing values up.
- Use `satisfies` instead of `as` to check a literal without widening it.

## Test placement

A unit test sits beside its owner as `<owner>.test.ts` or `<owner><Behavior>.test.ts`, following
[ADR 0007](../../shared/adr/0007-test-placement-and-fakes.md).

A layer guide may narrow this rule.

# Pi guide

Apply these rules with the [TypeScript coding guide](../../languages/typescript/guide.md) to every
file of a Pi package. They add to that guide and never loosen it. Each rule starts with its ID in
the [rules table](../../shared/rules.md).

Pi finds some files by path and keeps some names in saved sessions. Users, other programs, and saved
data depend on these names, so they follow the outside-surface rules of
[ADR 0008](../../shared/adr/0008-backwards-compatibility.md).

- `pi-discovered-path`: Declare every path Pi discovers, such as an extension entry or a skills
  folder, in the `pi` field of `package.json`. Keep each discovered path and skill folder name
  unchanged when you rename code. Change one only for its own reason, with a plan for existing
  users.
- `pi-registered-name`: Keep each name registered with Pi unchanged when you rename code. This
  covers tool names, command names, event types passed to `pi.on`, and custom entry types saved in
  sessions. Matching a function name is not a reason to change one.

If the file path starts with src/, apply: `core` holds the domain: its types, rules, and the I/O that every entry point shares. It depends on
no other role.

Also apply the rules in the project's AGENTS.md and the decisions in docs/adr/ that cover the change. Read them with file_read.
